loText: Describe operational resilience, identify the elements of an operational resilience framework, and summarize regulatory expectations for operational resilience.
question: A treasury analyst at a Canadian life insurance company is drafting an induction note for newly hired analysts that explains what operational resilience means and why it became a regulatory priority. Which of the following statements is the most accurate to include in the note?

options.A: Attention to resilience grew in the late 2010s, when regulators moved their focus from the operational stability of banks and insurers toward their financial stability.
options.B: Resilience covers the ability of firms and of the financial sector as a whole to prevent, adapt, respond to, recover from, and learn from operational disruptions.
options.C: Resilience concerns each firm’s own operations only, so disruptions at critical third parties such as cloud providers and central counterparties fall outside its scope.
options.D: Attention to resilience grew mainly from concern over market and credit losses, rather than from the industry’s critical dependence on IT systems and infrastructure.

solution:
Stem summary: Treasury analyst at a Canadian life insurer drafting an induction note on what operational resilience means and why it emerged.

**Concept and theory**

What it is. GARP defines operational resilience as the ability of firms and of the financial sector as a whole to prevent, adapt, respond to, recover from, and learn from operational disruptions. Two features of this definition matter. First, it is broader than a single firm: the regulator cares about the system, which is why the UK guidance repeatedly refers to harm to consumers and to market integrity. Second, the verbs cover the whole life of a disruption, before (prevent, adapt), during (respond), and after (recover, learn). loText: Describe operational resilience, identify the elements of an operational resilience framework, and summarize regulatory expectations for operational resilience.
question:
The chief risk officer of a Brazilian commercial bank is preparing a briefing for the board risk committee on how banks and regulators now view severe operational disruptions such as cyberattacks. She drafts the following statements:

I. Banks and regulators now accept that severe operational disruptions are inevitable, at least occasionally.

II. The focus has moved from a purely preventive approach to a balanced view of preventing, detecting, and correcting incidents so as to minimize their overall net impact.

III. Since severe disruptions are accepted as inevitable, preventive controls are no longer expected and the bank should redirect its control budget entirely to recovery.

IV. Extreme disruptions are now expected to be frequent, so the bank should plan for them as routine events in its normal operating budget.

Which of the statements are consistent with the regulatory view of operational resilience?
solution:
Stem summary: Brazilian bank CRO audits four statements on how banks and regulators now view severe disruptions.

**Concept and theory**

The old mindset. Classic risk management treated operational incidents mainly as something to prevent: build enough controls and the bad event should not happen.

The new mindset. GARP explains that, with the increase in cyber risk and several high-profile cybersecurity attacks, the industry’s mindset shifted toward accepting that severe operational disruptions are inevitable, at least occasionally. Schweser puts it the same way: extreme operational disruptions will occur, “but that they will be relatively infrequent.” Firms and regulators therefore moved from a purely preventive approach to a balanced view of preventing, detecting, and correcting incide […]

question: An internal auditor at a Japanese trust bank is reviewing a draft resilience policy. Each section of the policy is labeled with one of the components of operational resilience set out by the UK regulators. Which of the following section labels is NOT consistent with the content of the section it describes?

options.A: “Lessons learned”: a section requiring the bank to quantify the amount of disruption that could be tolerated for each of its critical services.
options.B: “Management of disruption”: a section on responding to disruption, keeping the trust of key stakeholders, and communicating clearly during a crisis.
options.C: “Important business services”: a section identifying the services whose disruption would cause intolerable harm to consumers or market integrity.
options.D: “Continuity of business services”: a section on mitigating the risk of disruption to critical business provisions, close to classic continuity planning.

solution:
Stem summary: Internal auditor at a Japanese trust bank checks which section label of a draft resilience policy does not match its content.

GARP notes that the UK regulators do not define resilience in one sentence. Instead they describe it through components. Learn them as five labels, each with one job:

| Continuity of business services | Business continuity | Closest to classic BCP; prevents and mitigates disruption of critical business provisions |
| Important business services | Key services | The innovation: a service-based view; identify services whose disruption would cause intolerable harm to consumers or market integrity |

question: A senior operational risk analyst at a UK building society is reviewing a project plan for meeting the UK regulators’ resilience expectations. The plan sets an impact tolerance for each of 140 internal processes, including the payroll run, the procurement approval workflow, and the archive of closed accounts, but it does not list any of the services the society provides to its members. Which of the following recommendations best aligns the plan with the UK regulatory approach?

options.A: Keep the process-level tolerances, because the UK approach extends classic continuity planning by setting a recovery objective for every internal process.
options.B: Drop the tolerances altogether, because impact tolerance is a qualitative board statement that firms are not asked to quantify.
options.C: Identify the services whose disruption would cause intolerable harm to consumers or market integrity, and set impact tolerances for those services.
options.D: Set tolerances only for processes that caused losses in the past, because the resilience approach is built on lessons learned from earlier incidents.

solution:
Stem summary: UK building society plan sets impact tolerances for 140 internal processes and lists no member services; choose the aligning recommendation.

**Concept and theory**

Process-based continuity. Traditional business continuity planning (BCP) works process by process: each internal process gets a recovery plan and a recovery time objective (RTO).

Service-based resilience. GARP calls important business services “the innovation of the regulatory approach to resilience.” The UK regulator “moved beyond a process-based view of continuity, to a service-based view.” Firms must:

(1) identify the services that, if disrupted, would cause “intolerable levels of harm to consumers or market integrity”; and

(2) ensure the continuity of these services within tolerance levels.

question: The risk committee of a German asset manager notes that the firm’s business continuity plan has been tested every year for a decade. A committee member asks which addition would most clearly move the firm from traditional business continuity planning toward operational resilience as described by the UK regulators. Which of the following additions best answers the question?

options.A: Strengthen preventive controls until disruption to critical business provisions can no longer occur, so that recovery planning becomes unnecessary.
options.B: Learn from the firm’s own incidents and from events made public at other organizations, and use them to keep improving against unanticipated extreme shocks.
options.C: Set a recovery time objective for each internal process, reviewed every year by the business continuity team against the latest test results.
options.D: Test the existing plan against more severe scenarios, because continuity of business services is the element that separates resilience from continuity planning.

solution:
Stem summary: German asset manager with a long-tested BCP asks which addition most clearly moves it from business continuity to operational resilience.

**Concept and theory**

Operational resilience grew out of business continuity planning but goes beyond it. GARP places the five UK components on a spectrum of novelty:

- Continuity of business services is “the closest to the classic approach of business continuity planning.”
- Important business services is “the innovation of the regulatory approach” (service-based, not process-based).

question: The chief compliance officer of a UK-listed general insurer is preparing a report for the audit committee that summarizes the UK regulatory expectations on operational resilience. Which of the following statements should she include in the report?

options.A: The FCA, PRA, and Bank of England issued the first regulatory guidance on resilience in 2018, and the new requirements sit alongside existing operational risk requirements.
options.B: The FCA, PRA, and Bank of England issued the first regulatory guidance on resilience in 2018, and the new requirements will replace the existing operational risk requirements.
options.C: The FCA, PRA, and Bank of England issued their 2018 resilience paper mainly to address the risks of remote working that followed the COVID-19 pandemic.

Stem summary: CCO of a UK-listed general insurer chooses the accurate summary of UK resilience expectations for the audit committee.

**Concept and theory**

Who and when. UK regulators were the first to publish regulatory guidance on resilience. The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), and the Bank of England (BoE) jointly issued a discussion paper in July 2018, Building the UK financial sector’s operational resilience, as the start of a comprehensive framework.

options.A: Governance forms the base, ORM is the central component, and third-party risk management and scenario analysis are the two supporting pillars.

question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian bank with a US subsidiary is checking a slide that summarizes the Federal Reserve’s 2020 Sound Practices to Strengthen Operational Resilience. The slide contains these statements:

I. The guidance views operational resilience as a key outcome of an effective operational risk management framework.

II. The guidance stresses the need to place operational resilience within a holistic enterprise management framework.

III. Third-party risk management supports resilience mainly by preparing the firm for tail events, while scenario analysis protects the resilience of supply chains.

IV. Since resilience is the outcome, a firm with a strong business continuity plan may treat resilience as a substitute for an operational risk management framework.

Which of the statements are accurate?

Stem summary: Internal auditor checks four statements on a slide summarizing the Fed’s 2020 Sound Practices to Strengthen Operational Resilience.

**Concept and theory**

GARP summarizes the Fed’s 2020 paper as running along similar lines to the UK approach (important business services, impact tolerance) and adding two framing points:

(1) operational resilience is “a key outcome of an effective ORMF”; and

(2) there is a need to insert operational resilience into a holistic enterprise management framework.

Schweser puts it as: an effective ORM framework would have operational resilience as the major result.

question: A supervisor at a national banking regulator is explaining to newly hired examiners how the Basel Committee’s 2021 Principles for Operational Resilience relate to operational risk management and to earlier national guidance. Which of the following statements is the most accurate?

options.A: Principles 3, 5, and 7 mirror the UK regulators’ approach, while Principles 4 and 6 mirror the elements highlighted in the Federal Reserve’s paper.
options.B: The principles were issued separately from the operational risk principles, to signal that the Committee sees resilience as independent of ORM.
options.C: The principles were issued together with the revised operational risk principles, because the Committee sees resilience as an outcome of effective ORM.

Timing and link to ORM. The BCBS principles on operational resilience came out in March 2021, at the same time as the revisions to the Principles for the Sound Management of Operational Risk (RPSMOR). GARP says this was intentional: Basel links the two topics, stating that “operational resilience is an outcome that benefits from the effective management of operational risk.” In its opening statements the BCBS makes clear that the robustness of an ORM framework is the first condition for a good level of operational resilience.

loText: Describe current practices by banks and supervisors in the governance of a cyber-risk management framework, including roles and responsibilities.
question: Angela Myer, FRM, works at Pinebridge Bank. She was recently reviewing the bank’s firewalls and safety measures erected to guard against cyber-based data theft. The exercise also entailed an in-depth outlook into the security processes in the bank. Ms Myer is most likely part of the bank’s:
solution:
**Concept**

Cyber-risk governance follows the three lines of defence. First line: business and IT functions that own and operate the controls. Second line: risk management and compliance, which set the framework and challenge the first line. Third line: internal audit, which gives independent assurance that the controls and security processes work.

**Exam trap.** Role-sensitive. “Reviewing” the adequacy of controls that others built and operate is assurance, which belongs to the third line. Building or monitoring them would be the first or second line.

loText: Explain and assess current practices for the sharing of cybersecurity information between different types of institutions.
question: The CRO at a bank wants to strengthen the bank’s capability to defend itself against emerging cyberthreats. To help achieve this goal, the CRO is assessing the current range of practices regarding the sharing of cybersecurity information between different types of institutions, as well as the potential benefits from sharing information. Which of the following statements would be most appropriate for the CRO to make?

options.A: The sharing of cybersecurity information among banks is less frequently observed and generally considered to be less effective than other cyber-security information- sharing practices.
options.B: The scope and depth of information-sharing practices among banks may significantly vary between financial markets, depending on the level of trust among participating banks.
options.C: Information-sharing among different national regulators has evolved significantly over the past several years and is now a widespread practice at a large majority of jurisdictions.
options.D: Existing peer-sharing mechanisms among banks focus on the exchange of information related to cyber-security incidents, but such information is generally not shared from banks to regulators.

solution:
**Concept**

Cyber-security information sharing takes several forms: bank to bank, bank to regulator, regulator to regulator and regulator to bank. Sharing among banks is the most common and depends on trust between participants. Sharing among regulators is the least common.

**Exam trap.** Each wrong option reverses which direction of sharing is common. Bank to bank: widespread. Regulator to regulator: rare.
